summary: Specifies the Host Identity Protocol, which lets hosts securely set up IP-layer state and separates the identity of a host from its address. This keeps communication going when addresses change. It uses a Diffie-Hellman exchange with public key identifiers and resists denial-of-service and man-in-the-middle attacks. It is experimental and was replaced by RFC 7401.

plainLanguage.summary: HIP lets two hosts agree on a cryptographic identity for each other, separately from the IP addresses they happen to be using. The identity is a public key, and the exchange that establishes it also agrees on a shared secret. Because the identity is a key rather than an address, a host can change address and keep the same identity, and a connection can carry on.

questions: what is a hip host identity tag
subtitle: Giving hosts a cryptographic identity so a session survives a change of IP address.

tldr.problem: An IP address names a host and also tells the routers where to send traffic, so a host that moves has to be given a new address, and any session it was running is tied to that address.
tldr.mechanism: HIP makes the public key of a host the identity that higher layers bind to, and uses a four-message exchange to establish shared state between two hosts. The exchange includes a puzzle the initiator must solve, which lets the responder stay stateless and resist denial of service.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5201 is an Experimental document from April 2008 and has been obsoleted by RFC 7401, which restates the Host Identity Protocol.

facts.label: Puzzle verification cost
facts.value: One hash computation by the responder

today: RFC 5201 is an Experimental document from April 2008, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 7401, which restates the Host Identity Protocol; the unit metadata also lists RFC 6253 as updating it. The RFC carries an IESG note listing the issues the working group expected future versions to address, including the use of SHA-1 and the requirement that an incoming packet's IP address be ignored.

sections.title: Why Separate the Identifier from the Address
sections.content:
The Host Identity Protocol lets consenting hosts securely establish and maintain shared state at the IP layer. The underlying idea is the same separation that other protocols pursue: an IP address does two jobs, acting as a routing label and acting as a name for the endpoint, and HIP replaces the second job with a cryptographic one.

In HIP the public key of a public and private key pair is the Host Identifier, and higher layer protocols bind to it instead of to an IP address. Because the identifier is a key, a change in a host's set of IP addresses can be authenticated directly between the two hosts, and strong authentication at the stack level becomes possible.

This document specifies the base HIP protocol, the four-message exchange that establishes the shared state called a HIP association before any communication takes place, together with the packet format and the procedures for updating an active association. Other parts of the architecture are in separate documents: using ESP for integrity protection and optional encryption, mobility and multihoming, DNS extensions, and a rendezvous mechanism for contacting mobile hosts. HIP is designed as an end-to-end authentication and key establishment protocol to be paired with ESP; it does not cover the fine-grained gateway policy control that IKE provides, and the RFC states plainly that HIP is not a replacement for IKE.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem HIP solves is that an address is not a name. If a laptop moves to a new network, it gets a new address and anything that tied sessions to the old one breaks. HIP gives the host a name of its own, a public key, and binds sessions to that instead.

sections.title: Host Identifiers and Host Identity Tags
sections.content:
The host itself is defined as the entity that holds the private key of the pair whose public key is the Host Identifier. Implementations must support RSA with SHA-1 and should support DSA; other algorithms may be supported.

The full Host Identifier is a public key, and public key algorithms differ in length, so it is unsuitable as a packet identifier or as an index into the operational tables a host keeps. Instead the protocol uses the Host Identity Tag, a 128-bit hash of the Host Identifier. The tag has three important properties. It is the same length as an IPv6 address, so it fits in address-sized fields in interfaces and protocols. It is self-certifying, meaning that given a tag it is computationally hard to find a host identity key that matches it. And the probability that two hosts get the same tag is very low.

The tag is generated by the ORCHID method, a SHA-1 hash over the public key with a fixed context identifier. The RFC is explicit that carrying host identifiers and tags in the header of every data packet would add overhead, so they are not expected in every packet; other means, such as the security parameter index in an ESP header, map data packets back to the right association. The HIP header is itself relatively large at 40 bytes, so it is expected to appear only in the control packets that establish or change association state.
sections.plainLanguage: The real identity is a public key, which is too big and too variable to put in a packet. So the protocol uses a 128-bit hash of it, the same length as an IPv6 address, and everything refers to the hash.

sections.title: The Four-Packet Base Exchange and the Puzzle
sections.content:
The system that starts the exchange is the Initiator and the other party is the Responder, and the distinction is forgotten once the exchange completes. The exchange has four packets. The first, I1, is a trigger: it carries only the Initiator's tag and, if it is known, the Responder's tag. The second, R1, starts the real exchange and carries a puzzle, the initial Diffie-Hellman parameters and a signature covering part of the message. The third, I2, carries the solution to the puzzle, the Initiator's Diffie-Hellman parameter and its own signature. The fourth, R2, is signed and finishes the exchange. The Diffie-Hellman keys are exchanged in the second and third packets, and the two parties are authenticated in the third and fourth.

The puzzle exists to protect the Responder against denial of service. The Responder supplies a random number I and asks the Initiator to find a number J such that a hash over the concatenation of I, the two tags and J ends in K zero bits. The Initiator generates candidates until it finds one, and the Responder verifies the answer with a single hash. The difficulty K can be set according to how much the Responder trusts the Initiator and how loaded it is. Because the puzzle is not covered by the signature, the Responder can keep a set of pre-computed R1 packets and send one of them, which is what lets it stay stateless and drop most spoofed I2 messages. The RFC recommends that a new puzzle and R1 be generated every few minutes and that an old puzzle be remembered for at least twice its lifetime.

The Responder's host identity is not protected in the exchange, and the Initiator's may be sent in the clear or encrypted with the Diffie-Hellman output. Both tags travel in clear text, so an eavesdropper who already knows the parties can check their identities. Data packets flow once the fourth packet is done, and the session keys for the association are drawn from the Diffie-Hellman keying material.
sections.plainLanguage: Four messages set everything up. The second one contains a small computational task, and the third must show the answer. Until that answer arrives the responder has done nothing but hash, so a flood of fake starts costs it almost nothing. The third and fourth messages also exchange the Diffie-Hellman values and the signatures that prove who is who.

sections.title: The HIP State Machine
sections.content:
The RFC describes the protocol as a state machine and gives a simplified diagram of the main transitions. A host with no association sends I1 and moves to the state where the first packet has been sent. Receiving an R1 and answering with I2 moves it on, and receiving R2 establishes the association. The Responder's path runs the other way: an I1 received and an R1 sent leaves it with no association, an I2 received and an R2 sent moves it to the state where the final packet has been sent, and the exchange completes from there.

From the established state, receiving a close message and answering with a close acknowledgement moves the host to a closing state, and so does a period of silence long enough to reach the unused association lifetime. In the closing state, a close acknowledgement received or a timeout moves the host to closed, and the closing message is retransmitted if no acknowledgement arrives. Eventually a timeout moves the host back to having no association. The RFC notes that the states in which the exchange completes can also be left by timeout, and that retransmission is used where a packet may simply have been lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The diagram names the stages: no association, first packet sent, second packet sent, final packet sent, established, closing and closed. Each incoming message moves the host to the right stage, and timeouts cover the cases where a packet is lost.

sections.title: The HIP Header
sections.content:
Every HIP packet starts with a fixed header. The first octet holds the Next Header value, the second the header length, the third a reserved bit that must be zero followed by the packet type, and the fourth the version, three reserved bits and a fixed bit reserved for compatibility with SHIM6. Then come the checksum and the controls, then the sender's 128-bit tag and the receiver's 128-bit tag, and finally the HIP parameters.

The header length field gives the length of the header and parameters in 8-byte units, excluding the first 8 bytes, so the minimum value is 4 and the maximum length of the parameters field is 2008 bytes. A receiver that meets an unknown packet type must drop the packet. The version is currently 1 and is expected to be incremented only for incompatible changes, since most extensions can be handled by defining new packet types, new parameter types or new controls.

The header is logically an IPv6 extension header, but this document describes only the Next Header value 59, the IPv6 no-next-header value, and implementations must ignore trailing data if some other value arrives. HIP packets are carried in IP protocol number 139, which IANA has assigned to the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Each HIP message carries a fixed 40-byte header: two octets of control information, a checksum and controls, and the two 128-bit tags that say who sent it and who it is for. The rest of the message is a list of typed parameters.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HIP is designed to authenticate hosts securely and to limit exposure to denial of service and man-in-the-middle attacks. In doing so it is itself subject to those attacks, which the RFC acknowledges could be more damaging to a host's ability to do business than the attacks it prevents.

Five denial of service scenarios are described. A spoofed I1 can tie up an initiator that is evaluating the R1 and building the I2; the defence is to ignore any R1 for which no matching I1 was sent. Once the puzzle is solved, an attacker can send spoofed packets with invalid payloads or bad signatures and consume the Responder's resources; the defence is to discard further I2 packets from that Initiator's tag after a set number of bad ones, at the cost of possibly dropping valid ones. A spoofed I1 that looks like a peer rebooting produces an unexpected R1, which is dropped. Replaying old R1 packets can make an initiator solve stale puzzles, which the R1 generation counter is designed to prevent. And a spoofed close message can be used for reflection if the receiver answers it with an ICMP message.

Man-in-the-middle attacks are hard to defend against without third-party authentication. The protection HIP offers is indirect: if the Responder's identity can be obtained from a signed DNS zone, a certificate or another secure source, the Initiator can use it to validate the R1, and the same works in reverse for an Initiator with a non-anonymous identity. The RFC also warns that NOTIFY messages are informational and unacknowledged, so a host should not change state on the strength of one, and that ICMP messages should not be acted on too eagerly, since a spoofer could use them to break up an exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: HIP defends against attacks on the handshake, but the handshake can be attacked too. The RFC lists the ways: faked start packets, fake second packets, replays of old challenges and spoofed close messages, and says how each is answered.

messages.label: I1: trigger exchange
messages.note: Carries the initiator's tag and, if known, the responder's tag.

messages.label: R1: puzzle, Diffie-Hellman value, key and signature
messages.note: The responder can pick this from a set of pre-computed packets and stay stateless.

messages.label: I2: solution, Diffie-Hellman value, key and signature
messages.note: Without a correct solution the message is discarded.

messages.label: R2: signature
messages.note: The exchange is complete and data packets flow.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: Only the value 59, the IPv6 no-next-header value, is described. Implementations must ignore trailing data for other values.

fields.name: Header Length
fields.desc: The length of the HIP header and parameters in 8-byte units, excluding the first 8 bytes. The minimum value is 4.

fields.name: Reserved bit and Packet Type
fields.desc: One reserved bit that must be zero, followed by the 7-bit packet type. A packet with an unknown type must be dropped.

fields.name: Version and reserved bits
fields.desc: The 4-bit version, currently 1, then three reserved bits that must be zero and one fixed bit reserved for SHIM6 compatibility.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: A checksum over the HIP header and parameters.

fields.name: Controls
fields.desc: Control bits carried in the HIP header.

fields.name: Sender's Host Identity Tag
fields.desc: The 128-bit hash of the sender's host identity public key.

fields.name: Receiver's Host Identity Tag
fields.desc: The 128-bit hash of the receiver's host identity public key.
